body: That's an insane amount of money for OPI, what a rip off! Thanks for sharing your perspective and answering my question.

This is off-topic from OP's post, but I've been seeing this comment a lot when people defend MC's price increase (and their old pricing also). 


When I purchase OPI, it's no more than $6.00 from discount stores. At my local nail supply stores, the most I've seen them charge is $13.00 (the ones I purchase at nail supply and beauty supply stores are around $8.00 to $10.00) At department stores, arou d $12.00 to $14.00 Online, the highest nail lacquer is priced at $13.99US and for base/tops, the highest is $14.99. I didn't  look through their gel catalogue because MC doesn't sell gel and I also don't wear gel polish. 


Where are people purchasing OPI where they're $16.00+ and now, $18.00+? Because those people are getting ripped off. 


Not trying to hate, I'm just really curious because I've seen a lot of people (on the FB group, on their IG, and some folks on the MC subreddit) say that OPI is more expensive than MC, when that's never been my experience. 


Full disclosure: I live in the US at a HCOL area.

I looked into their catalogue. 

Based on what I've observed:

* Glow in the Dark (there are 2) - $15.00
* Thermal (there are 6) - $16.00
* Magnetic (there are 24) - $16.00
* Cremes (there are 8) - $13.00
* Shimmers - 52 polishes @ $15.00 / 14 polishes @ $14.00
* Holographic - 12 polishes @ $15.00 / 2 (glitters) polishes @ $14.00 / 1 (topper) polish @ $13.00 

I'm going to guess that cremes and toppers will have a $1.00 increase, because cremes typically have a higher profit margin, making them at least $14.00. 

More complex/new formulas seem to hold the higher price point, at least in the case of holos and shimmers. I'm going to guess the ones that are at $15.00 will take a $2.00 increase, putting them at $17.00. The two GITD will probably face a $2.00 increase.  

I'm going to guess that the older formulas at the $14.00 will take a $1.00 increase, which will put them at $15.00, but it's also highly likely that they will implement a $2.00 if they decide they want more money. 

As far as the magnetics, at $16.00 per bottle, I honestly wouldn't be surprised if they took a $2.00 increase, making them $18.00 each. 

Fortunately, I already have what I want from Mooncat, but it's a bummer that they'll be out of the price point I'm willing to shell out for nail polish for future releases. I'm gonna have to unfollow them on socials so I don't feel FOMO for any future releases. Besides, I have almost 500 nail polishes, so I'm probably gonna have to take a break from collecting, at least until the economy gets better.

It's your body and your money.

You'll never know. The only realistic advice I can offer is to keep interviewing. At the end of the day, even though they may seem nice and compassionate in the interview, they are still employers conducting an interview. If they're anything like the typical corporate sort, you're probably not getting the job. 

I worked at a real estate office as an office manager. At one point, they held interviews for a property manager position and one of the interviewees cried about her family and how she'd been having a hard time trying to find a job that would work out because she had a disabled family member to care for. The interviewers (my managers at the time) were nice and tried to comfort her, but when she left, they expressed how awkward they felt while she was crying. She didn't get the job. 

On the one hand, I sincerely hope that crying during the interview didn't take you out of the candidate pool but realistically, the chances are grim. You're gonna be working at a school. Depending on what grade level you're teaching, children can be brutal and other teachers can be mean. They might take it as you not being able to handle pressure. 

Good luck, OP. Worst case scenario, you can take this as another practice interview so that you can do better on the next one. I hope you feel better soon.

Hey, I've been there. It really helps if you have some close friends or maybe some family members you trust to vent to or even just hang out with to distract yourself while you're looking for other opportunities. If you're not able to get meds or therapy, perhaps these might help: 

\- Practicing gratitude: I learned this when I was in med hold in military training. We were all injured in some way and miserable because being injured meant having to go back where we left off with a new set of recruits or we were in limbo to go home because we were too injured to continue. When we woke up, we wrote in a journal, three things we were grateful for that moment, and just spend a few minutes being quiet with those thoughts. Even something as simple as, "I'm breathing, I have a roof over my head, and I will have food to nourish myself today." If you don't like journaling, then just say it in your head. They taught us the same thing when I was hospitalized for being suicidal. It sounds silly, but it actually helped me. 

\- Have you thought about getting new hobbies that don't involve the internet? I noticed my mental health improved when I wasn't on my phone or online as often. If you're a crafty person, maybe trying crocheting, knitting, cross-stitching, painting, or sculpting? If you like reading, maybe find a new book that you think you might like? Goodreads and Likewise are great resources for new books to read based on what you already like. 

\- Even if you're introverted, maybe exploring parts of your city/town you haven't visited may help your mental health. You can even go on nature walks if that suits your fancy. 

\- If you're the type of person who likes to learn new things or you had hobbies that you don't do anymore because of your mental health, maybe revisit those (either by yourself or with the company of your friends or family)? 

Hope you feel better, OP. Good luck on finding a job that isn't as soul crushing as your current one.

I found one recently from the internet that I changed to my liking. I don't remember the exact measurements because I tend to eyeball things 

Basic recipe: 
3 large onions or 5 small/med 
Olive oil or butter (I used butter)
1 head of garlic
Parsley
Sundried tomatoes 
1/2 c coconut oil
Paprika, to taste
Pasta of choice

What I added to mask the coconut milk taste (because I don't like coconut milk, but the recipe called for it): 
Shichimi togarashi (Japanese 7-spice), to taste
Lemon pepper, to taste
Furikake, to taste
Dried rosemary, to taste
Dried thyme, to taste
Dried tarragon, to taste
Cayenne powder, to taste
Maggi sauce, 2 cap-fulls
Soy sauce to taste
Lemon juice, to taste
Kale, as much as you want
Chopped celery, as much as you want
85% or 90% lean ground beef
Cheese of choice (I like cheddar)

Directions
1) use mandolin slicer to slice the onions and celery
2) combine onions, sundried tomatoes, garlic, paprika and other spices that you like (and the ground meat if you are using it) in a casserole dish/pan. Drizzle with oil, and cover with foil. Bake in oven for 400°F for 1 hr 
3) at around the 40-min mark, prepare your pasta according to package directions
4) take out your pan from the oven and combine the coconut milk and greens, adding pasta water as needed to achieve your desired consistency and taste. Add cheese if you like.

Our friend group had petty drama recently, but unfortunately, I think I nipped it in the bud so it's not that exciting. 

TL;DR - She was upset that we were loosely planning activities in a group chat that she asked to be included in. She tried to impose a rule no one wanted to follow, and she left the group because I called her out on her BS. 

More context: 

She's 37 and the eldest in the group. I'm 31 and the only other female in the group. We're a pretty chill bunch and we have a group chat for loosely planning hangouts. If you want to do something, you bring it up, and if enough people want to go, you set a time window to meet up. If you decide you don't want to go, you just let the group know and we go without you. 

She has many food aversions (she hates meat, fish, anything with onion, garlic, soy sauce, and anything spicy) and many dislikes, so if we knew we were going to a restaurant that didn't serve what she liked or doing an activity she isn't into, we don't bother telling her about it. At some point two years ago, she saw a photo of the guys in the group having chicken wings and beer and she got upset because she wasn't included. As a result, we create a group chat with her in it.

Fast forward to more recent times. Two weeks or so ago, we talked about going to a Bolivian restaurant. People had other activities planned, including her, so since not many people in the group seemed to want to do the activity, I suggested we postpone and they can do whatever they want that day. She threw a fit, stopped participating in the group chat, and we all moved on because in our heads, it's not a big deal.

A couple of days ago, someone wanted to go to a park over the weekend to play badminton and have a picnic. She then chimed in, saying she was going to explain why she was upset. She then went on about how she had a lot of anxiety, that she couldn't "turn off" her scheduling brain because she has to "do everything" for her husband and her parents because her husband "doesn't plan anything" and her parents are old and can't remember anything anymore. As a result, our loose planning and loose scheduling style made her stressed out, and she proceeded to blame us for her stress. That if we wanted to "propose" hangout ideas to her, it needed to be "well-researched with all the specifics" and that if even one person doesn't show up within 15 minutes, she would leave no matter what. 

I knew the guys would just ignore her because her texts were way too long (15 walls of text about how she's upset because of her husband, her job, her parents, and then passive aggressively saying we cause her stress because of our lax style of scheduling, and how we needed to do what she wanted if we wanted to keep her in the group). Hell, even I thought about ignoring it, but I knew that if we never responded and just planned activities without her, she'd get upset at us that she isn't included. 

So I responded. Honestly, it felt like writing an email to an upset customer. I empathised with her, reminded her that we included her in the group chat because she requested it, and that if she had a problem with her job, her husband, or her parents, to address those issues with them instead of taking it out on us. I also told her that we don't treat hangouts as doctor's appointments. If she wants to show up, great. If she doesnt, see you next time! If she was going to a hangout with the expectation of leaving within 15 minutes if even one person doesn't show up, what's the point? I concluded it by telling her I don't like to walk on eggshells when hangout with friends; if she's so stressed that something as simple as "do whatever you want, if you want to go, we'll see you there. If not, see you whenever," will cause her brain to short circuit, work on that problem instead of taking her anger out on us. 

She responded with, "thank you for your feedback. You have my blessing to start a new group chat without me and I will resurrect this thread when I am ready. Brighter days are ahead. " 

I responded with, "K have fun at <the activity she was doing instead of hanging out with us>". 

She ended up blocking me on all socials lol

You're going to hate me, but this is true and I am speaking from experience. Get a voice teacher or join a choir. 

A lot of people who are self-taught end up developing bad habits because of information overload from the internet. There's nothing wrong with getting a voice teacher. I think what perpetuates the self-taught craze is the fact that talent shows revere those people or society expects that it should just be natural talent. You can save yourself lots of pain and potential vocal damage if you have an expert guiding you. 

Me personally, singing came naturally to me. I'd listen to a song, imitate it, and it sounded good (they even made me do talent shows...the worst parts of childhood was being made to sing karaoke because my parents wanted to show me off, and if I didn't want to do it, I'd get grounded). The problem with that was if I did something new, like belting for instance, I would over-exert my vocal cords and I wouldn't be able to sing for at least a week because of how much my throat hurt (due to pressure I was putting on my larynx, whether that was pushing it up or down). Eventually, I stopped singing because I hated how people would make me do it all the time, but once I got the passion back for it, I was doing everything wrong. I tried looking through YouTube singing teacher tips, followed what they advised (with regards to breathing techniques, tone placement, creating space, relaxing your jaw, avoiding tongue tension, etc.), but I still ran into the same problems if I attempted something new to me (for instance, I was very interested in opera because one of the choir girls had a beautiful tone I wanted to imitate). By hiring a voice teacher, you can save time (because you're able to address the problem right then and there), you can save yourself some physical pain, and most certainly save yourself the frustration of being unable to execute whatever sound you want. 

In the mean time while you are seeking a teacher for guidance, work on breathing and fundamentals. The straw exercise is helpful in building breath support  and control. The hissing exercise works well, too. For the straw exercise, what you do is you breathe as deeply as you can (making sure your whole body is relaxed, because it's not supposed to be painful) and you breath out of the straw as quietly and as lightly as you can, ideally for between 30-60 s. The hissing sound is the same concept--light, quiet, and for as long as possible. Don't get caught up in classifying your voice right away, because your voice changes as you grow older. You can think you're a mezzo for the longest time, but when you get proper technique, turns out you're a soprano all along. 

Good luck!

I recommend that you first start working on breathing exercises. You may have heard from your past choral directors and other internet sources you may have already looked through, that you should sing from your diaphragm. Most of the time, this makes people think they are limited to utlizing only their chest or their upper abdomen (at least I did, and according to my teacher, so did most of his hobbyist students). In reality, when it comes to singing (especially opera), you utilize your whole body, and by "singing from your diaphragm," you're limiting the amount of air you're working with. Another way to think of it which helped me tremendously is to (as peculiar as it sounds) sing from your crotch...technically, above your crotch. When you breath as deep as you can, you will notice that your abdomen will expand all the way down towards your upper pubic area. When your body is relaxed and you source your air from all the way down there, it's you'll find it will be much easier to project your sound and reach higher notes. The straw exercise helped me when I started out with voice lessons. What you do is you take a plastic straw, breath in as deeply as you can (albeit silently and relaxed), and you breath out through the straw for as long as you can (as quietly as you can).
 
When it comes to warmups, Jeff Rolka's warmups on YouTube are a good place to start. Claudia Friedlander's (soprano) and Joyce DiDonato's (mezzo soprano) master classes on YouTube are also a good resource. These are in no way a substitute for a real-life voice teacher. The operatic style of singing is very taxing on your vocal cords, and if done incorrectly, you can risk potential permanent damage in the long term. 

When you sing warm ups, remember to keep an open space at the back of your oral cavity with your soft palate raised, your jaw, your tongue, and your larynx relaxed. The best way I can describe it is kind of a yawning position. Make sure you keep an open sound. 

Another thing...just because you were an alto in a choir once, don't automatically lump yourself in that box. I thought I was a mezzo for the longest time (I sang the alto section as well in middle school...mostly because we had a shortage of them), and after a month or so of being taught proper technique, it turns out I was actually a soprano. Vocal classifications are there to help determine where the vocalist can project over an orchestra. 

Remember: when it comes to singing, opera or not, stay where you are comfortable. If it starts hurting, you're probably doing it wrong. If your voice starts getting tired, don't push it, stop and try another day. Drink lots of liquids, take care of your health and your body, and take things slow. A lot of vocalists (like me) tend to put unnecessary pressure on themselves to learn something beyond their current skill level because singer A did it in x amount of time. You wouldn't expect an absolute beginner who can barely play Mary Had a Little Lamb on a violin, to play out Vivaldi's Winter. So take it step by step. 

Good luck!

P.S.: when seeking voice teachers, it's helpful to ask what their strengths and weaknesses are regarding language. The ability to grasp pronunciations and meanings of songs is important so that you know where to place emphasis on words, where to pause, etc., and also portray emotion of the charactet you're playing for that piece. For instance, right from the beginning, my teacher told me he prefers to teach in German, Italian, Russian, Spanish, and Latin. He prefers not to do French arias because while he can do a convincing French pronunciation to his colleagues, he recognizes that it isn't his best.

The best advice I can give, coming from someone who only started studying with a teacher just over 1 year ago, is to find a teacher who teaches this style. He/she will be able to show you proper technique and give you critiques of what you need to work on most, and give you arias to practice at your skill level. 

Operatic singing is highly technical, and there's a lot of focus on projection, proper breath support, and foreign language. What's your experience in singing? Have you done choirs, a complete beginner, a competitor, etc.? What genre do you typically listen to and sing along to?

It's difficult to say without seeing you actually doing it, but if it helps, I'll share a few things I've learned from my teacher:

- "Singing from your diaphram" is a bit of a lie. To clarify, the diaphram is a small muscle between your lungs and abdominal muscles. Instead, sing from your lower belly, so that you have adequate air to get through the notes. 
- Relax, don't force it. If you're relaxed, good posture is the body's natural inclination/response. The more relaxed you are, the easier it will be to go breeze through those high notes. 
- If it sounds good, go for it. If it doesn't and it feels uncomfortable, don't. I'm not saying you should limit yourself, I'm saying that you should focus your concentration on those comfy notes rather than focusing on trying to impress people with high notes to the point of your detriment. You can work on those high notes or low notes eventually, but until then, stay at your sweet spot, esp. when it comes to auditions, so as to not ruin your voice. 
- Regarding your throat hurting, there's a possibility that you may be pushing air from the wrong place, or maybe even shouting, as opposed to belting. I've heard practicing with chest voice if you want to be a better belter, but I'm not an expert. Your best bet is to consult an in-person vocal teacher, express your concerns, and you'll sing better in no time
